speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head V of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the Budget Debate, Members in the House have reminded us that growing the economy is not an end in itself, but a means for us to build better lives and better opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we also know that ensuring that we always have that means that is continuously growing and yet inclusive is certainly no mean feat.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the Minister for Finance has said in his Statement, our path ahead will not be easy, especially in light of the major shifts happening around us, such as a changing global economic landscape, the emergence of new technologies and our own demographic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a way, we saw it coming, which is why since the start of this decade, we embarked on the road to restructure and transform our economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the early phase of restructuring, the Government tightened foreign labour inflow and nudged wages higher for our local workforce and pushed for productivity improvements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It has inevitably caused pain to some businesses although there were also various assistance schemes introduced, such as the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) scheme, and support for skills upgrading to help mitigate the impact and to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If the 2017 small and medium enterprises (SME) Development Survey is any indication, we may have passed the most painful phase of economic restructuring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Twenty-twelve is the year when foreign labour tightening was introduced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, many businesses bit the bullet, made the difficult adjustments and changed their business model in response to the tightened labour market environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Wages have risen and we have also seen credible improvement in overall productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding, there will be companies which are still struggling and adjusting, some of which are cyclical in nature.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am glad that this year's Budget continues to extend help to businesses facing near-term challenges with the continuation of assistances like the Wage Credit Scheme (WCS), the Corporate Income Tax (CIT) rebate and the deferment of the increase of foreign workers' levy (FWL) rates for two sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Workers, too, went through the difficult transitions as companies restructured.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The continual need to upgrade and convert to new skills has become part and parcel of working life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to do more to help workers facing career transitions and this Budget also strengthened support for workers under the Adapt and Grow Initiative.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, the next phase of the economic transformation efforts now zero in on fostering pervasive innovation, building deeper capabilities and forging strong partnerships riding on the already launched Industry Transformation Map (ITM) platforms.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Innovation is the way to go for businesses to stay competitive in the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is starting from a position of strength as we already have a critical mass of high-tech sectors, a vibrant startup and financing ecosystem, world-renowned universities and research institutions and a strong global pool of research scientists and engineers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To foster pervasive innovation, especially for the SMEs, the Budget enhanced various schemes supporting companies to innovate across the entire value chain.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I look forward to hearing more details about the PSG from the Minister later and how this streamlining would improve support for businesses seeking new solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another new idea from the Budget is the Open Innovation Platform (OIP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To be piloted this year, it is an online crowdsourcing platform set up to help businesses find partners to co-create solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many smaller companies may not have the resources to seek partnerships to co-develop solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This platform can facilitate easier collaborative work among SMEs on joint innovation initiatives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope this can help plug the missing link with regard to translating research outcomes into viable commercial opportunities and thereby produce a new breed of innovative global companies in Singapore following the commercialisation of the IPs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I look forward to hearing more details from the Minister as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On building deeper capabilities, the Budget signalled the shift away from broad-based measures, such as PIC, to a more targeted and innovation-focused approach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do agree that in this next phase where we deepen transformation, a more customised and slightly more flexible approach will yield better results.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the impending merger of Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING) Singapore and IE Singapore into Enterprise Singapore, it makes logical sense to streamline the Capability Development Grant (CDG) and Global Company Partnership (GCP) into the new workhorse now known as Enterprise Development Grant (EDG).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can the Minister share how the new integrated EDG can better support companies to deepen capabilities?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Digital capabilities will be the new competitive advantage for businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The adoption of digital technologies can transform business processes, improve productivity, and help SMEs export products and services more easily.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With digital technology, even the smallest SME can have the opportunity to export its products and services globally, hence, expanding their growth frontiers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are good opportunities in the digital space in the region.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, besides China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) can also be a strong potential growth market in e-commerce for companies to explore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are already various support schemes for SMEs to adopt digital technologies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clearly, there is significant room for more SMEs to move forward and to use digital technologies to enhance competitiveness and to grow their businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, developing digital capabilities does come with investment costs and risks, but not going digital may well be an unviable position soon.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is better to take some risks now, learn the right lessons.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If it does not work out, do recognise that this is a continuous journey of upgrading.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While we hope that more SMEs can be involved in the ITMs, we should be realistic that in sectors where there is a very large base of SMEs, it is not possible to have everyone on board from Day 1.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, the companies can also be proactive to come forward, with the trade associations and chambers (TACs) playing the key role of raising awareness and facilitating the deeper involvement of ITMs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My last point is about skills and jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the business landscape changes, we need to ensure that skills of our workers remain relevant and our skills training can respond quickly to emerging skills and tech disruptions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, how is the Government helping the professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) who have been displaced or who wish to move into growth sectors the Government has identified?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Prime Minister Lee mentioned during Chinese New Year, productivity and economic growth are still mainly concentrated in manufacturing and export-driven sectors.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because of this, the general sentiment on the ground is that many SMEs which are not related to these two sectors are less optimistic and feel as though they are still in a recession, even as we mention that our economy is expanding.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, I would also like to ask the Ministry on how it can help make our economic growth more broad-based.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Henry Kwek, you can take both cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My first cut is on riding on rising Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Despite the global uncertainties, Asia is cited as a region of high growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What are the Government's plans to help Singapore companies take advantage of a rising Asia?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government elaborate on the specific measures that we are doing for key growth markets within Asia, as well as for the various growth sectors?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government also share about the broad-based measures that we are doing to encourage Singapore companies to internationalise, and for our people to take on international careers within growing Asia?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any pressing gaps that our industries and workforce face that must be addressed?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, can the Government share on the progress made to strengthen our Asia-specific market research firms mentioned in previous Budgets?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Much has been said about ASEAN's potential – youthful demographics, large population, and sizeable headroom for growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But those can only be achieved if ASEAN member states work together to unlock the potential.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, given ASEAN's dynamism, we have also seen rapid economic improvements in many bright spots within ASEAN, so Singapore cannot take for granted our economic hub status within ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, Singapore must always work hard to shape the economic architecture of ASEAN, so as to benefit ASEAN and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And this is especially so, given our responsibility as ASEAN Chair this year.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share on our efforts to unlock this potential to benefit Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Besides positive economic conditions, Singapore companies and citizens must also be ready to seize opportunities within ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What more is the Government doing to ensure that we have prepared to capture the opportunities created?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, in my Budget speech, I talked about getting Singaporeans to think ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the various Government agencies can look into that.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, we have been a keen proponent of the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC).

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It was during the 13th ASEAN Summit in 2007 when Singapore was last the ASEAN Chair that the blueprint to establish AEC was adopted.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For Singapore, AEC is not just an aspiration, but also a strategic necessity, to mitigate the geopolitical risks of the region being mired in economic under-development and political instability, and the region becoming divided and caught among the great economies of China, India and the US.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is now ASEAN Chair again and we are in a good position to facilitate the economic integration.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This seems to be rather low key, compared to the work that is needed to push forward the already-delayed AEC.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Does the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) have a more concerted plan to develop the AEC while Singapore is ASEAN Chair?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What can Singapore do to better integrate the most important sectors in the region, for example, the electronics sector, especially in the context of the other major shifts in the disruption caused by new technologies?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sun Xueling, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even though the 6% growth rate may not be high by historical standards, Asia is expected to continue outperforming the rest of the world by a significant margin.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In India, Prime Minister Modi's administration is pressing ahead with reforms aimed at enhancing the business environment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: China’s 13th Five-Year Plan demonstrates its leaders’ commitment to rebalance demand and revive productivity growth through a more competitive market-based allocation of resources.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In ASEAN, there has been a ramping-up of public investments through various infrastructure projects.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The region around us is gearing up to provide its citizens greater prosperity and greater opportunities for foreign direct investments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since decades ago, Singapore’s fortune has been closely tied to the region.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our local business community is active in the region and many family businesses have networks across Asia.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With Technology and rising consumerism, the population in the region is seeking new products and services.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Their young population’s rising incomes and skills also mean that they are participating in the region’s supply chain in a new way.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, with these changes happening in Asia, how does Singapore and our companies leverage new opportunities and what are the Government’s plans to help Singapore companies take advantage of a rising Asia?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: ASEAN is a major hub for manufacturing and trade, as well as one of the fastest growing consumer markets in the world.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is one of the largest economic zones, with growth being rapid and relatively stable for the past two decades.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although Asean is becoming more integrated, investors have shared about local preferences and cultural sensitivities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A one-size-fits-all corporate strategy can, therefore, not be applied across widely varying markets.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With Singapore helming ASEAN's chairmanship for 2018, we have a chance at positioning ASEAN for a more seamless economic region, as well as strengthening a focus on innovation and the digital economy.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how are we working with ASEAN member states to unlock this potential to benefit Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Looking at the figures, this economic growth is impressive and the poverty rate amongst our neighbouring countries has been declining.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When ASEAN Vision 2020 was established, one of the key objectives was to enhance economic growth and deepen intra-regional trade ties with the free movement of people, goods, services and investment capital in ASEAN.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As it stands, the ASEAN intra-regional trade is still weak.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While Singapore is one of the most open economies in ASEAN, our trade with other ASEAN states is just about a quarter of our total trade.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In a world that is becoming more protectionist and mercantilist, there is all the more reason for ASEAN to accelerate economic integration.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Can the Minister share what are some of the challenges to this integration?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Based on conventional wisdom, it is likely that having an open, competitive and integrated ASEAN implies better chances of new industries to establish in our part of the world.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If this outcome is within reach, how then can our workers tap upon this opportunity to expand their working scope and skills?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Events of recent years showed that we cannot take for granted the expansion of free trade because the world would not see a reversal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: MTI's continued vigilance to remove barriers as Singapore businesses have to access overseas markets is worth lauding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: First, I strongly support the achievement of CPTPP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is a significant development to add to the current positive momentum seen in Singapore's trade prospects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Modified agreement is also significant because it demonstrated progress which should not have been possible without a deep engagement throughout the original TPP process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the deep engagement by our trade negotiators will now have to be translated into tangible footholds by our businesses looking for internationalisation opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, SMEs still faced significant challenges when competing beyond Singapore, especially if they were not set up with such potential strategies in mind in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: How different would the prospects of CPTPP be for SMEs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And has the engagement process that enabled the transition from the failed TPP agreement to the revised CPTPP throw up specific opportunities which we can prepare SMEs for?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For companies looking to take advantage of opportunities to internationalise, it is important for them to develop capacity along the trajectory to match the broader direction of changes occurring under the ITMs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is this potential for making such a linkage between free trade agreement (FTA) negotiations in general and the CPTPP, in particular, actively pursued as part of the ITM strategy?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, you have two cuts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In some Western economies, FTAs are being viewed negatively.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have seen the recent political mood in the US regarding TPP.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some politicians in the US have even proposed that existing long-standing FTAs like the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) should be renegotiated.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What are Singapore's options, and what are Singapore’s trade priorities?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, what balance of bilateral FTAs and regional FTAs should we be aspiring for?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, some of my Clementi residents have worked in regional markets in ASEAN, or they have counterparts from other ASEAN countries whom they meet through the course of work.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My young residents speak of the growing economic buzz in ASEAN, the energy and dynamism, especially in the major cities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Also, a certain hunger and will to succeed among young people in the youthful populations of our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This growth and buzz pose opportunities for Singaporeans to forge partnerships, find new business partners and new business opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But some Singaporean friends are also worried about whether our businesses can keep up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They worry about business overheads and the cost structure in our domestic Singapore economy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, some have mentioned land costs and rental overheads.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These are issues that I have spoken about during the Budget Debate and I mentioned a few possible alternative models for approaching land rental and land cost allocation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, developing a vibrant manufacturing sector is important for our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to multinational corporations (MNCs), we need to ensure the success of local startups and Singapore SMEs in manufacturing, as these may, with supportive policies, be more likely to keep Singapore as a centre of gravity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Mr Koh Poh Koon recently shared data on rental costs in reply to my Parliamentary Question (PQ).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The percentage of rental out of total costs may not be high now, but it may rise if technology replaces manpower in the future, as may happen with the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Industrial rentals have also seen volatility in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And Singapore does not have low land cost zones on the outskirts as other global cities may have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will MTI consider setting a target for industrial rental inflation to stay in line with the consumer price index (CPI) and adjust policies accordingly?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will MTI also thoroughly benchmark industrial rentals in other cities with big manufacturing startup sectors and manufacturing SME sectors and publish the findings?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Henry Kwek, you can take both cuts together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The recently released Annual Economic Survey showed improved economic performance in 2017.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: However, there was variation among sectors in performance and outlook.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can the Government provide a broad overview of how the various industries are doing in terms of performance and outlook?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Which sectors have high growth potential, and which are the ones that require significant transformation and restructuring?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: It is important that we set the appropriate aspirations for various sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Also, how is the Government supporting the different industries to deal with their unique circumstances?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: In our ITMs, have we been able to bespoke our policies for various industries?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Moving forward, will we be able to have greater policy differentiation, for example, in terms of manpower policy, than what we have today?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The ITMs are the cornerstone of our restructuring efforts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Since 2015, we have rolled out most ITMs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can the Government provide a comprehensive update on our restructuring efforts?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can the Government also share some of the early successes of restructuring?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Which sector has achieved rapid restructuring and which sectors have been lagging?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: And what is the main reason for the differing restructuring speed?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Specifically, I would like to ask the Government for an update on the Lifestyle ITM.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Having said that, I would caution everybody against measuring our restructuring success using solely output economic indicators, such as value-add productivity change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: This is because it will take a few years, sometimes three to four years, for outcomes of new strategies to show up in output statistics.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: So, using solely output statistics now to gauge the success is not wise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, can the Government also share more on specific initiatives, which are more input indicators rather than economic output indicators, that are designed to aid restructuring?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck, you also have two cuts, can you take them together?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Mr Chairman, forming ESG has been good news for the business sector, and many TACs and businesses have called for a single agency to focus on supporting local businesses.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We have nearly 200,000 SMEs and they are at different stages of growth, ranging from startups to micro-enterprises, medium- to large-sized companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It will not be easy and impossible to assist all of them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The first principle of business is to be self-reliant and build a business that is commercially viable that there is demand for your products or services.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Companies should actually manage your expectations when it comes to grants and schemes and expectation of a single agency like ESG.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Competitiveness is as important as self-sufficiency and both form the essence of what we call the first principles.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We have to find a position of not too little and not too much, and that should form the approach; a middle way for economic planners and companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This middle way between extravagance and want implies a view of the balance sheet that looks for long-term profitability rather than short-term success.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And it should be closely linked to the idea of self-sufficiency.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: ESG should then play a facilitating role to help kickstart ventures, support international growth as a focus, and develop capabilities for the companies and strengthen them to compete.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It should be less about grants than the need to change for the enterprise to scale and grow.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: These are what will really help the companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Could the Minister share what ESG would do for enterprises at different growth stages and also ideas on internationalising Singapore's SMEs?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: However, this has also caused uncertainty as to whether the different types of grants that cover different gaps will actually be covered by a single grant.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: For example, there are different grants that are available today, such as the automation grant under CDG.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The aim is to automate processes but there are issues as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The data has shown that equipment manufacturers made up the majority of the payments.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, could the Minister share how SMEs have actually benefited from this grant and how SMEs from other areas have also benefited from this grant, and whether productivity in these respective companies has actually increased?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: There is also a grey area where equipment manufacturers could potentially push for more sales and use the grant to upsell their equipment.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, these are the processes that should be tightened.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Submission of claims has also been an issue for some.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: However, if the project cannot be seen through to completion by the SMEs, a penalty could be considered to be in place, if they fail to meet the required milestones.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, integrating all the grants into a single grant for ease of access and application is the step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We believe that this will develop the capabilities of the companies better and more effectively.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Along with the grant portal, and ESG as the administrator, we believe that this will help streamline many of the processes.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Could the Minister elaborate how such integration could benefit companies and review examples of how it could help?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Many large companies or MNCs, both foreign and local, have set up their base in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And this not only provides jobs but opportunities to grow our local SMEs through partnership with the large companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And since the setup of PACT, there have been examples of such partnerships in the areas of innovation, capability, upgrading and knowledge transfer.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Most importantly, the scheme provides long-term business opportunities for the SMEs with the larger companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I believe that the programme can still expand and be enhanced to support more partnerships across different sectors.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Not all sectors you could actually enhance and some partnerships cannot be forced.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Some of these large companies can also help the SMEs, not just by providing volume of business but consultancy, for example, in digital marketing or branding.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And such public relations branding and digital marketing are somehow knowledge that is lacking in many of our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Could the Minister share with us how PACT has been performing so far and how would the integration benefit the companies in future?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   This year’s Budget affirms the important role of TACs in driving industry transformation and upgrading.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Besides initiating the establishment of the Trade Association Hub, the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI) also set up the Trade Association Committee (TACOM) led by the business community.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The business community welcomes the many assistance schemes rolled out in this year’s Budget to help in uplifting the capability of enterprises.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, businesses are concerned, compared to large enterprises, how much have SMEs contributed to productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Just how effective have local SMEs been in upgrading themselves?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this year's Budget, the Government has introduced a new assistance scheme, the PSG.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is very different from the PIC and ICV schemes that businesses were familiar with.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: What is good about PSG is that when companies have identified a suitable productivity upgrading project, they could apply immediately.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is different from PIC’s tax deduction option at year-end.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, from 1 April this year, businesses could apply directly for PSG through the Business Grants Portal set up last year.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, one integrated scheme could help enterprises to improve internal capabilities as well as to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, enterprises look forward with great anticipation to the newly set up ESG, hoping that it could achieve an outcome of 1+1 equals more than two.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Besides helping enterprises to improve their competitiveness and internationalise, services provided by ESG should include coordinating manpower resources and improving technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This would make it easier and faster for firms to apply.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses also welcome the launch of the ASEAN Leadership Programme.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: ASEAN countries have always been the key overseas markets for local businesses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This programme would be very helpful in enabling local entrepreneurs and senior management to better understand market trends.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget has also included the PACT scheme, the aim being to encourage partnership or collaboration among companies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: One way is to let big companies help smaller enterprises improve their capability.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, local enterprises could tap on this scheme to nurture a mutually cooperative business culture and develop regional ventures together.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, some businesses have expressed concern about certain new measures.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, with effect from next year, the Government will implement a new carbon tax to encourage reducing carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Although businesses realise that Singapore aims to become an even more liveable and sustainable city, and that we need to protect the environment, they are concerned about the impact on their costs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, as their industry counterparts abroad do not need to be taxed in this way, local enterprises could become less competitive.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We are, nevertheless, glad to know that the Government has also committed that, in the first five years of introducing the carbon tax, revenue collected would go towards giving more grants and support to companies to enhance energy efficiency and reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I have also received feedback from some startup companies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They hope that even if profits were to be generated in the first five years of setting up the company, corporate income tax should be waived, enabling them to plough back the revenue into operations and carry out the initial phase of development without a hitch.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Over the past few years, the role of industry associations in industry transformation has received sound affirmation from everyone.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, trade associations will continue to strive hard towards the implementation!

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, under the enhanced Local Enterprise and Association Development (LEAD) programme, the Singapore Food Manufacturers' Association (SFMA) has already set in motion a series of industry development projects for the benefit of its members.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Will other industry associations also benefit from LEAD?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I noticed that this year’s Budget did not give specific mention to the SME Centres.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I wonder what role the SME Centres, previously set up by SPRING Singapore, are expected to perform as we move ahead.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Even if they do not expand overseas, they have a strong social function in creating employment opportunities, and I hope the Government would not ignore them.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can do even more to create a more favourable business environment for micro-enterprises and SMEs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding their small size, this could enable them to become small but exquisite, small but nimble, small but beautiful, and small yet highly competitive.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Eventually, SMEs must continue to learn ceaselessly and develop capabilities.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Chairman, Sir, the PACT scheme has been operating since 2010.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It has been enhanced and extended a number of times to cover more sectors and co-innovation activities.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The scheme seeks to support collaboration between large corporations and local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The question is how successful has the PACT scheme been?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: In my view, as this scheme is oriented towards a win-win partnership between large corporations and SMEs, with the aim of transforming the capabilities of SMEs, the crux of the success lies in whether the SMEs gained in a transformative manner.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: In answer to past PQs, some figures have been given by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But how many of these SMEs saw their capability transformed?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: What metrics does the Ministry use to measure the transformation?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: In a 2014 article published on SPRING Singapore's website, the article looked at how Keppel Shipyard joined PACT to improve the capabilities of its SME vendors and contractors.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But this so-called success was defined in terms of productivity gains from the view of a large corporation and nothing was said about the capabilities of the SMEs and whether these were transformed.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Capability transformation of SMEs should be directed towards their empowerment to seize regional and international opportunities, rather than to be limited to serve the needs of large corporations based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: To this end, it would be good to know the profile of the large corporations benefiting from PACT to date, whether these are largely Government-Linked Companies (GLCs) or MNCs, and whether more could be done to link up local SMEs to international supply chains through PACT.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, next, the setting up of the Infrastructure Office to seize the opportunities being opened up by the One Belt One Road Initiative is timely.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: During the Budget, the Minister announced that an Infrastructure Office will be set up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is to help Singapore firms to tap on infrastructure opportunities in Asia, including China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I strongly believe that the Government should do more to develop local companies in the construction sector so that we can benefit from the booming infrastructure projects in the region.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One of the ways to do this is to help our local companies to build track records.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If there are no track records, how to go overseas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Give them a helping hand, groom local consultants and contractors and give them opportunities to participate in large Government-led projects in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In cases like that, has the Government thought of how to involve the local companies instead of just having them as smaller players down the value chain?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They may possess the skills, capabilities and willingness to invest, but due to their lack of a track record, they have difficulties in venturing abroad.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some had done better and become subcontractors of MNCs and doing work overseas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government is serious about helping the local companies, I am sure you can find out more information from members of the Singapore Contractors Association.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I had an earful when I met up with them recently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am pleased to note that the Government plans to strengthen its funding support through the PACT scheme.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is to encourage firms to forge regional collaborations and internationalisation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that through this scheme and the Infrastructure Office, there can be greater encouragement and fostering of deeper partnerships between Government agencies, major companies in Singapore's construction industry, and contractors from the smaller companies, so that everyone gets a share of the pie.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, this will result in an overall increase in quality and reputation in our construction sector.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, to encourage more construction companies to internationalise, there are a number of possible solutions to make this option more accessible and appealing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One way is to help our companies to understand the tax regime of foreign countries that they are interested in.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Taxation in foreign countries can be quite complicated.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are very afraid of running into problems in foreign countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And many companies also do not have deep pockets and cannot afford to go through the steep learning curve.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has a comparatively small domestic market that is extremely competitive.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As such, for our local companies and businesses, especially our SMEs, to be able to achieve sustainable growth, they need to take advantage of external opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There has been a great push by the Government on internationalisation and the opportunities abroad that Singapore companies can take advantage of.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, many SMEs in Singapore face financial and manpower constraints to do so.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If an SME is to venture abroad, there is a lot of groundwork or "homework" that needs to be done first.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For example, before breaking into a new market, they will need to undertake market research, navigate the business and regulatory environment and make the necessary investments in order to put themselves in the best possible position to succeed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These are the challenges our SMEs face even when an opportunity to venture abroad arises.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Sakitiandi, you can take both cuts together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, going overseas will mean facing many challenges for the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because of their size, they are more sensitive to the uncertainties and the risks of going international.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of these companies were initially set up without plans to go abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, from paid capital, manpower, marketing and branding and perhaps even the operations and logistics were principally set with focus on the local market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are thus not prepared for the task overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is just one thing when they get the grants and the guidance from the Government agencies to go international.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is another challenge to get them mentally prepared and build up their confidence to branch out overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To venture into a different market where the language, cultural and religious preferences are different, not to mention taxes are different, not to mention the work ethos, the social and political infrastructure and legal systems, invariably, it takes a much, much longer time for something to develop, especially when you have to put applications through to the Government Ministries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, internationalisation is necessary if an SME wants to grow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But apart from all the support from the Government, there needs to be a mindset shift among our SME entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can I ask if the Minister can give some outline of the assistance in the pipeline to help our SMEs in this area?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The more efforts or channels we have, the better.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, we have often heard of various Government schemes to help our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And these range from various grants to other assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, not all SMEs are ready to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of their key concerns include the size of their business capital and their stomach to take risks when going abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their logistics and manpower may also not be up to speed to go international.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Others are still grappling with issues, such as productivity and technological disruption.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, maybe more help can be targeted for heartland SMEs and help for merchant associations to disseminate the wide range of complex programmes that are already available to help them overcome future challenges or maybe something akin to the Pioneer Generation Ambassador (PGA) programme on the ground but for businesses.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And as in any investment, there should be proper returns.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have previously spoken on the need for us to track our R&D outcomes, monitor the impact, as well as to think of better ways in which we can improve.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, this cut, Sir, will focus on a few issues.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Governments around the world have found ways to do so.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the US maintains the Interagency Edison (iEdison), which is a unified electronic data system used by more than 30 US federal funding agencies. iEdison receives, stores, tracks, sorts, monitors and generates reports of inventions and patents that have resulted from awards, extramural grant or contract funding.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For newly designed programmes, or in the case of a prolongation of an existing programme, an ex-ante evaluation will assess the rationale of public intervention, formulate a range of objectives and suitable instruments, and assess the impact of Government-owned intervention.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Evaluations are carried out solely by external organisations that are selected through a call for tenders.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And elsewhere in other places like the United Kingdom (UK), Hong Kong and so on, third parties have been commissioned to undertake evaluation of R&D investments.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, we need to have more upstream measures to better R&D decisions and downstream measures to facilitate tech transfer and IP commercialisation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the useful practices in other countries include the use of patent analytics and landscaping which are aimed at informing policy discussions, strategic research planning and technology transfer.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if you take a look at what Taiwan has done, they have the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) and it actively developed strategic mapping of IP and patent analytics.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It institutionalised IP mapping along its R&D process where researchers are required to do IP mapping or landscape mapping before they embark on an R&D project.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to know what is already there and do not reinvent the wheel.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Also, the institute conforms new inventions to the industry's needs through IP mapping, along with patent review procedures to strengthen quality and practicability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: ITRI has won awards at R&D 100 Award each year since 2005 and they have built a sizeable portfolio of more than 20,000 patents, the quality of which could be evidenced in their successful patent lawsuits against Samsung in 2009 and out-licensing deals to major companies like Mitsui.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that, in Singapore, the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) is also building up its capability for patent landscaping and investigations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In China, researchers are able to work for companies that buy their research for up to three years while maintaining their positions at the institute where they did the research.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is to incentivise researchers to conduct R&D with a view to commercial application instead of merely academic application.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, this will also, if we adopt it here, allow us to have a more market-driven and more market-sensitive research.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There is much that Singapore can do in learning from different countries.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There are many proactive efforts going on, so I would like to ask for clarification from the Government in a few areas.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Government categorise the different areas of R&D and what are these categories?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In respect of each category, what are the indicators used to track our returns on R&D investments?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What are the commercialisation rates of our technology transfer offices?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Excluding researchers, what are the employment numbers that have been generated in Singapore, for Singapore industries, as a result of R&D outcomes over the last decade for what we have spent?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How has Singaporean researchers progressed and benefited from collaborations with external researchers, again, over the last decade?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What is the social economic impact that has been achieved by R&D investments and, specifically, in which industries, sectors and for which groups of persons?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What are the practices in place to ensure better economic outcomes from our R&D investments?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From my questions, I am sure it is clear that I am driving at not just economic but also socioeconomic impact.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that when the Government sets out key performance indicators (KPIs) as well as measurables, we would take those into consideration.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, there should be also greater duties on the part of institutions receiving grants to cooperate with the Government by furnishing information and by giving data, so that we are able to build the necessary landscaping.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The development of Singapore's R&D and innovation capabilities has been a key economic strategy for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A series of plans had been implemented over the last three decades to position Singapore as an innovation-driven, knowledge-based economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With Singapore's investments in R&D rooted in the need to upgrade and strengthen the competitiveness and growth of the economy, it is critical that such investments translate into tangible economic outcomes and impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Although public-sector research at our universities and the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) institutes has grown in intensity and excellence, it is less clear how these national research capabilities have translated into business innovation that will yield economic competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There have been various measures, including this Budget, aimed at translating our public sector research efforts into commercially viable applications.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: MNCs seem to dominate many R&D-intensive industry clusters, such as electronics, pharmaceuticals and biomedical sciences.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is critical that we institute a framework for the transfer of capabilities and expertise from MNCs to the local ecosystem, while creating good jobs in the local economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, MNCs, large local companies (LLCs), SMEs as well as startups have different needs and capacities for engaging in R&D and research output.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We, therefore, must foster a flexible partnership ecosystem that caters to companies’ diverse circumstances such that all types of enterprises in Singapore may benefit from R&D.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With innovation at the centre of Singapore’s next phase of economic development, the urgency of investments in R&D to deliver value and support industry transformation efforts is more critical than ever.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There should be clear KPIs set for research projects to measure how they contribute to value creation in terms of economic and societal outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, it was announced in October last year that the Government will be launching the Open Electricity Market (OEM) this April.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: This is a positive move as it will allow households and businesses the ability to buy electricity from a retailer which has price plans which best meet their demand.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: While OEM will initially operate in Jurong during the soft launch phase, it was also announced that this would be extended to the rest of Singapore in the second half of 2018.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: While I support the opening up of the electricity market, I am concerned that consumers may be faced with numerous price plans and permutations, and this may get very confusing for them.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: We need to put in safeguards to ensure that Singaporeans are no worse-off with the OEM than they were when there was no choice.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: The OEM is something which will be very new to the vast majority of Singaporeans and we need to be able to give Singaporeans the confidence that this is a move that will benefit them.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: More generally, would the Minister be able to provide any updates on the soft launch of the OEM in Jurong, and also let us know what consumers can expect when the OEM eventually rolls out?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In some sectors, it is higher, substantially higher.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Presumably, in the food and beverage (F&B) services sector, rentals also account for a substantial portion of business costs for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Commercial rentals have decreased over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Looked at conversely, for these particular SMEs, high rental costs remain a challenge even in an environment of falling rentals.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It would not be far-fetched to think that in this minority of SMEs that remain most concerned about high rentals, many are in the retail and F&B services sectors.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: These businesses have a special importance in shaping our living environment and contributing to our quality of life.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Innovation in their service offerings and business processes bring benefits that are felt immediately by the community.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry consider targeted assistance, for example, rental rebates directed at qualifying startups and SMEs in retail and food services, so as to bring added diversity and vibrancy to our heartlands?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Chairman, even as I often speak up to champion more support for SMEs, I would like to acknowledge the significant efforts on the part of the Government and call on SMEs to seize the support provided to transform their businesses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: A slew of programmes has been launched over successive Budgets in the last few years to help SMEs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Some are very generous indeed, such as PIC and WCS.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: This year, we continue to see more Budget measures targeted at SMEs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: A long list – Corporate Income Tax Rebate (CITR), EDG, DTDI, OIP, PSG, SME Digital Tech Hub, tax reduction for IP registration and the list goes on.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, I am making the point that the Government is really making an effort.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: This is with the aim of providing better support to industries and enterprises in their new phase of growth to build capabilities, innovate and go international.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I am heartened to see many traditional businesses transform as they tap on Government schemes and embrace new technology, automate, innovate and internationalise.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Despite being a 40-year-old business, the transformation journey started about five years ago when the attractive PIC provided great incentives for them to upgrade their kitchen equipment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The company received support from SPRING Singapore to automate their kitchen processes, while JTC provided the much-needed central kitchen space to consolidate eight sub-scale kitchens operating across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: With a more efficient operation, the company has reinvented itself and seen unprecedented growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: With automation, they are now better able to keep long service senior staff as manual work is kept to a minimal.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The modernisation of their business has also enabled them to attract an amazing team of younger leaders passionate about inventing new food products, opening new retail outlets and striking new partnerships to capture more market share.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The Government schemes can always be better, but there are many programmes already out there that can make a difference to your business.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, amid the major shifts spelt out during the Budget Statement, the Minister for Finance announced a slew of initiatives to support our SMEs overcome near-term challenges and to ride on future opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Grant applications are also streamlined so that SMEs can better tap on Government assistance.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some employees, especially those in the SMEs, are worried that they will be replaced with automation or when the company goes through transformation, and they may no longer be needed at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From our experience in the Labour Movement, there are some encouraging stories and some learnings.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, SMEs in the retail industry were encouraged to adopt technology and make use of Government funding.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the facilitation help of our team in U SME in the Labour Movement, some of the retailers in the SME sectors have adopted radio-frequency identification (RFID) in their retail outlets.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Previously, staff need to manually do stocktaking but, with RFID, they could just use the scanner to find out the stock numbers easily.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, Mr Chairman, it is with "right" technology rather than "high" technology that helped ease our SMEs and their workers into adopting transformation at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through such interactions and others that we had, it is clear that some of the SMEs and workers are still tentative in adopting more automation.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Labour Movement is thus concerned with the readiness of our workers in the SME side to adopt and adapt to the new technology that is forthcoming.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our familiarity with the workers has also proven to be invaluable when it comes to helping them adapt to the transformation that is occurring.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Support is already readily available to help businesses which wish to innovate and adopt technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do they navigate through all the new initiatives and identify what is relevant to plug their current gaps?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do they, as bosses, help their workers to be digitally ready, especially among the older workers?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Have we been effective in ensuring that workers in SMEs are geared up to uplift their employability and readiness to adopt technology?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The LEAD programme has provided resources for many TACs to upgrade their secretariat services and general services, as well as implementing several different schemes for the Government and the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: TACs are an integral part of transforming the different sectors.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: To me, they are actually the catalysts for things, like the ITMs, to effect the change in the sector itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Although the membership base of many of these TACs is not representative of the entire sector, most of the major companies, I believe, are members of these sectoral or general trade associations.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But we need to make sure that whatever schemes that the trade associations implement and the LEAD grants that are given to trade associations are effectively used and allocated.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We have to make sure that the KPIs set for them are at the level where the impact is felt at the sector level and also at the enterprise level.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: However, they will need greater support as well from the Ministry, especially when we have the ITMs coming on board for so many different sectors.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In the manufacturing sector, the advent of new technology is challenging traditional manufacturing processes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Manufacturing companies, especially the SMEs, sometimes struggle to stay competitive and relevant in the face of technological advances in their processes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: However, instead of fearing change, we should encourage our SMEs to take advantage of the opportunity to grow by embarking on innovation and the adoption of technology.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The question, however, is how can we help them to do so?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We are all aware that the Government has many schemes in place to help SMEs in this area.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: These include broad-based technology adoption to the granting of financial support.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: However, in the face of a wide array of options in Government support, on top of the overwhelming breadth of technology options available, many companies just simply do not know where to start.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Many SMEs also do not have a good sense of where their internal processes stand in terms of readiness and suitability to adopt smart technologies and processes to begin this transformation process.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As a result, some can get disillusioned and disappointed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This was largely driven by the chemicals, electronics and precision engineering cluster sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While having a rosy manufacturing performance is something we can cheer about, the concern will always be how long this cycle will last.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I note that the electronics sector is likely to continue performing, given the strong external demand for semi-conductors and computer peripherals, but there are other sectors that we would have to review, like the transport, engineering and biomedical clusters, that continue to be on the decline for several quarters.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In the early 2000s, the Government made a big push for biomedical and life sciences in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Soon after, we expanded and attracted companies to begin their manufacturing activities here.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As with every industry and business segment, the landscape evolves with time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The current decline in the cluster is not because the biomedical sector is becoming a sunset industry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Rather, the drag was from pharmaceutical manufacturing, which is volatile, while biomedical devices manufacturing is thriving and remains attractive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The question is how does MTI review the diversity of business segments within each cluster and ensure an optimal balance in business portfolio within the cluster to support local employment over time?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This is fundamental to our long-term strategy and, possibly, the lever that is most impactful to our ITMs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Does MTI continue to review these businesses after they are established or have insights as to how the businesses are managing to meet future new challenges, say, within each five-year period?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The impact on business continuity these days is no longer confined to business readiness but their ability to respond and foresee potential threats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Given shorter business cycles, the rise of technology disruptions and potential political sanctions, the possibility of businesses being displaced is higher.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As a result, it will be difficult to have an executable ITM framework if the fundamentals are not firmly plugged in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I know the ITM needs to be a living document, one that allows elements within the industry to be added, changed and adapted to new landscapes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: On the other hand, it will be difficult to scale up and have effective transformation throughout each industry cluster should there be a need for the base framework to be adjusted constantly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In today’s context, most industry cycles are cyclical in nature, including the emerging technologies, which themselves are volatile.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: On the same note that I have made earlier, the need to understand the industries better also has a bearing on how well-prepared our workers are for future industry evolvement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Unless we have more clarity on the longer strategic plan about the type of industry sectors in Singapore that we plan to pursue, we may end up in frequent pursuit of roles playing catching up.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While we can entice companies to set up shop in Singapore, our workforce needs to be ready with the necessary capabilities in good time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Further, how can our workers effectively transform and switch from one industry to another over a short period?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I hope MTI will consider the points raised and share the strategic plans for Singapore’s industries.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Mr Chairman, we have been building up our startup landscape in Singapore for some time now, and our drive to attract the best startup talent to Singapore is slowly paying off.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: At last year's Committee of Supply (COS), MTI announced initiatives to enhance the startup scene, including the unification of Government support schemes for startups under the Startup SG umbrella, as well as the streamlining of the EntrePass Scheme to allow us to attract more talent.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: So, there has been observable progress in what we are doing for startups.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Tech startups operate in a wide range of industries and generally look at how technology can help us work smarter and more quickly.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The pace in startups is normally very quick and it is well-known that the majority of startups will fail.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Yet, many still enter the startup world with grand plans on how they can change people's lives for the better.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: What is probably a sad truth of this ecosystem is that there are likely to be failed startups which actually have very good ideas.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: And if they had done things slightly differently, they really could have made a difference to the people's lives with their products.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: It is undoubtedly a tall order, but is there any way that we can help to identify and support these sorts of startups with good ideas but which have failed for reasons other than having a poor product?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: For Singapore to thrive in the startup space and for us to attract the best startups, we need to continually keep our pencils sharp and be relentless in seeking new ways to keep Singapore front of the minds of startup founders when they are looking for places to establish their businesses.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: We have made progress in these endeavours and I would like to ask the Minister if there is more in the works which will make us even more competitive and which will help us support and attract startups.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Has there been any feedback on the initiatives which were announced and rolled out last year and what is the Government's assessment on the success of these initiatives to date?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have two cuts, please take both cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Chairman, I would like to ask how the Government is helping PMETs who have been displaced or wish to move into growth sectors identified by the Government.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Many displaced PMETs were previously working in mid-level management, which is particularly susceptible to cost cutting as advances in technology have allowed for easier coordination of work tasks.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: For example, previously, a company might need more mid-level managers to disseminate information and coordinate work tasks.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: But now, with platforms, such as Whatsapp, a single manager is able to instantaneously disseminate the information to the rest of the workers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Many PMETs who find themselves displaced became drivers for Grab or Uber.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Would the Ministry elaborate what are the schemes available to help such PMETs?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: The ITMs emphasise the importance of our companies seeking out opportunities in the region.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Last year, many of our ASEAN neighbours have GDP growth rates which are higher than the 3.6% reported in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: The Philippines, Vietnam and Myanmar reported 6.7%, 6.3% and 7.7% GDP growth rates respectively.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Closer to home, Malaysia and Indonesia reported 6% and 5.1% respectively.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Very often, we hear of Singapore companies, which have done well at home, only to lose money when they venture out.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: To take advantage of the growth in regional economies, our Singapore companies will need to acquire a deeper knowledge of regional markets, not just of foreign rules and regulations, but also industry-specific knowledge, as well as important information, such as the reputation of potential business partners.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: As such, I would like to ask how MTI is equipping our Singapore companies with the relevant market knowledge.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I declare my interest in speaking on this topic as the President of the Consumers' Association of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Two years ago, during the COS debate on consumer protection, I spoke on the need to ensure that consumers are protected when making purchase transactions online.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that consumers who buy online would have to agree to the arbitration clause when transacting with these companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These consumers will have no negotiating power to ask for the arbitration clause to be removed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For many of these consumers, their transaction values are usually of a quantum well within the limit of $10,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, if a consumer buys a surface laptop through the Microsoft website and for some reason they have a dispute, they would not be able to seek recourse through SCT because of their arbitration clause.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Likewise, if they were to shop at Shoppee and buy a Nintendo set or earpiece or another laptop, they also will not be able to seek redress through SCT because of the arbitration clause.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the Second Reading of the SCT Bill in 1984, the then Second Minister for Law and Home Affairs Prof S Jayakumar said: "The primary purpose of this Bill is to provide for a speedy and inexpensive machinery to handle small claims arising from disputes between consumers and suppliers." I humbly submit that the rationale for SCT still holds true today and is valid.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, this will make a mockery of the rationale for the SCT if the jurisdiction of SCT can be easily ousted simply by inserting an arbitration clause.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is also timely for MTI to review the entire framework and to consider more legislation to provide protection for consumers in respect of online transactions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
